prompt:
Extract every policy commitment stated in the text below.

Rules:
- One commitment per line.
- Write each as a verb phrase: an action followed by its object. For example: "raise the income tax threshold" or "build 300000 new homes".
- State each commitment at the level of a distinct policy action, not its implementation details. Do not subdivide a single commitment into steps.
- Include every commitment. Do not select, rank, prioritise, or judge importance.
- Use the text's own terms for policy objects. Do not substitute synonyms.
- Do not number the lines. No bullets, headings, preamble, or commentary.
- If the text states no policy commitments, output the single word NONE.

<text>
New Labour sets out a programme of national renewal rooted in shared values, modern means and practical results. It rejects the old left’s statism and the Conservative right’s laissez-faire, offering a politics for the many not the few, governed by a bond of trust: promise only what can be delivered—and deliver it. The aim is a confident, one‑nation Britain with world‑class education and healthcare, safer streets, a modern welfare state of rights and duties, a dynamic economy, clean politics, and leadership in Europe and the world.

Economic stability is the platform for rising living standards. New Labour will keep inflation low (matching the 2.5% target), reform the Bank of England to secure credible, accountable monetary decisions, and follow strict fiscal rules—borrowing only to invest over the cycle. There will be no increase in the basic or top rates of income tax; the long‑term goal is a 10p starting rate; VAT on domestic fuel will be cut to 5%. A windfall levy on excess utility profits will fund a welfare‑to‑work drive to move people from benefit to employment. The approach is save to invest, not tax and spend.

Partnership with business will boost competitiveness: tougher competition law, revitalised public‑private investment in infrastructure, targeted help for small firms, Regional Development Agencies, support for science, design and new green industries. A sensibly set national minimum wage, determined with advice from a Low Pay Commission, will end the worst excesses of low pay while maintaining a flexible labour market; key union law reforms of the 1980s stay, with fair recognition where majorities vote for it.

Education is the number one priority: smaller infant classes (funded by ending assisted places), nursery places for all four‑year‑olds, a relentless focus on literacy and numeracy, “setting” by ability, technology in every school via a National Grid for Learning, stronger teacher training and professional standards, lifelong learning through a University for Industry and Individual Learning Accounts, and fair, income‑related student maintenance repayments.

The NHS will be rebuilt by ending the costly internal market, cutting red tape and reinvesting savings in frontline care—treating more patients and ending waits for cancer surgery. Primary care will lead local, multi‑year commissioning; there will be annual real‑terms funding increases, a new public health lead, a ban on tobacco advertising, and an independent Food Standards Agency.

On crime, New Labour is tough on crime and its causes: halve the time from arrest to sentencing for persistent young offenders; get police back on the beat; decentralise the CPS; crack down on disorder; introduce new offences for racial harassment; coordinate action on drugs with testing and treatment; strengthen victims’ rights; and give Parliament a free vote to ban all handguns.

Family life will be supported by a national childcare strategy and family‑friendly work rights; housing security through anti‑gazumping measures, safer rentals (licensing HMOs), “commonhold,” tackling homelessness, and investment from council house receipts. The basic state pension is protected; stakeholder pensions will expand secure second‑pension coverage; SERPS remains an option; carers gain fair credit; and a Royal Commission will propose fair funding for long‑term care.

Every department will be a green department. An integrated transport policy will strengthen rail with a new rail authority and better regulation, deliver a public‑interest partnership for the Underground, improve buses and road safety, and promote cleaner vehicles. Culture and sport will be backed through NESTA, school sports, and lottery reform with a not‑for‑profit operator.

Politics will be cleaned up: end hereditary peers’ voting rights; reform party funding and ban foreign donations; incorporate the European Convention on Human Rights; enact Freedom of Information; hold a referendum on Commons voting reform; devolve power to a Scottish Parliament and a Welsh Assembly (by referendums), create a London mayor and authority, empower regions and local government.

Britain will lead in Europe—completing the single market, enlarging the EU, reforming CAP/CFP, signing the Social Chapter, safeguarding key vetoes—and will decide on the single currency by hard‑headed economic tests and a referendum. Defence remains strong through NATO, Trident retained within a multilateral disarmament agenda, a strategic defence review, a ban on anti‑personnel landmines, UN reform, a new Department for International Development, renewed aid and debt relief, human rights at the core, and leadership against climate change.

Five pledges:
- Cut infant class sizes
- Fast‑track punishment for persistent young offenders
- Cut NHS waiting lists by treating 100,000 extra patients
- Get 250,000 under‑25s off benefit and into work
- No rise in income tax rates; cut VAT on heating to 5%; keep inflation and interest rates as low as possible
